t:
(a) 
Section 165 of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to employees trusts) is hereby amended by adding at the end thereof the following new subsection:


“(d) 
Certain Employees’ Annuities.—Notwithstanding subsection (c) or any other provision of this chapter, a contribution to a trust by an employer shall not be included in the income of the employee in the year in which the contribution is made if—

“(1) 
such contribution is to be applied by the trustee for the purchase of annuity contracts for the benefit of such employee;


“(2) 
such contribution is made to the trustee pursuant to a written agreement entered into prior to October 21, 1942, between the employer and the trustee, or between the employer and the employee; and


“(3) 
under the terms of the trust agreement the employee is not entitled during his lifetime, except with the consent of the trustee, to any payments under annuity contracts purchased by the trustee other than annuity payments.

The amount so contributed by the employer shall not constitute consideration paid by the employee for such annuity contract in determining the amount of annuity payments required to be included in his gross income under section 22 (b) (2); except that if the tax imposed by this chapter for any taxable year beginning before January 1, 1949, has been paid by the employee with respect to such contribution for such year, and not credited or refunded, the amount so contributed for such year shall constitute consideration paid by the employee for such annuity contract. This subsection shall have no application with respect to amounts contributed to a trust after June 1, 1949, if the trust on such date was exempt under subsection (a). For the purposes of this subsection, amounts paid by an employer for the purchase of annuity contracts which are transferred to the trustee shall be deemed to be contributions made to a trust or trustee and contributions applied by the trustee for the purchase of annuity contracts; the term ‘annuity contracts purchased by the trustee’ shall include annuity contracts so purchased by the employer and transferred to the trustee; and the term ‘employee’ shall include only a person who was in the employ of the employer, and was covered by the agreement referred to in paragraph (2), prior to October 21, 1942.”



 
    (b) 
The amendment made by subsection (a) shall be applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1938.

fable.w: This is a tax provision excluding certain employer contributions to annuity trusts from employee income. The tempting reading is that the "written agreement" and "consent of the trustee" language signals participation, but those are private arrangements between employers, trustees, and employees, not consultation with outsiders before a federal decision. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.
fable.s: pursuant to a written agreement entered into prior to October 21, 1942, between the employer and the trustee, or between the employer and the employee

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to define the tax treatment of certain employee annuity contributions. It establishes criteria for when such contributions are excluded from an employee's taxable income. There is no requirement for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties before a federal decision is made. The text deals strictly with statutory definitions and tax liabilities.

opus.w: This section changes the Internal Revenue Code to say when an employer's contribution to an annuity trust counts as the employee's income. It sets no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking authority, consultation, or right to sue. The written agreements and trustee consent it mentions are dealings between private parties, not outsiders taking part in a federal decision, so the keyword 'agreement' does not make this participation.
opus.s: such contribution is made to the trustee pursuant to a written agreement entered into prior to October 21, 1942, between the employer and the trustee, or between the employer and the employee
opus.b: The tempting misreading is to treat the "written agreement" between employer and trustee, or the need for "the consent of the trustee," as outside parties taking part in a federal decision. That fails because those are private arrangements between employers, trustees and employees. No federal agency or official has to consult anyone before deciding something. The section only sets rules for how employer contributions to annuity trusts are taxed.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to define the tax treatment of certain employee annuity contributions. It does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a decision. The agreements mentioned are private contracts between employers, employees, and trustees, not interactions with the federal government for the purpose of influencing a federal decision.
qwen_chat.s: a contribution to a trust by an employer shall not be included in the income of the employee in the year in which the contribution is made if— (1) such contribution is to be applied by the trustee for the purchase of annuity contracts for the benefit of such employee; (2) such contribution is made to the trustee pursuant to a written agreement entered into prior to October 21, 1942, between the employer and the trustee, or between the employer and the employee; and (3) under the terms of the trust agreement the employee is not entitled during his lifetime, except with the consent of the trustee, to any payments under annuity contracts purchased by the trustee other than annuity payments.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "written agreement" between employer and employee or trustee implies a participatory process. However, this is a private contractual arrangement for tax purposes, not a consultation with the federal government before a federal decision. The section defines tax treatment, not a government decision-making process involving outside parties.
